title: Skill Integration — An Overview

pts: Communicative competence names the full set of abilities needed for real communication, not grammar alone.
It includes grammatical, sociolinguistic, discourse and strategic competence as distinct, interacting components.
This model is the theoretical spine Tier II's methodology is built on.
points.who: Dell Hymes; Canale & Swain's model of communicative competence

items: Choose one unit from the coursebook you teach.
Mark each exercise by the competence it mainly develops: grammatical (G), sociolinguistic (S), discourse (D) or strategic (St).
Count the marks.
Discuss with a colleague which competences are well served and which are almost absent.
Add one activity for the weakest competence.
A teacher circle audits one unit per grade and compares results across Classes 6–10.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Describe an object from the lesson without saying its name. Your partner guesses.

blocks.x: Coursebooks lean towards grammatical competence because it is easiest to exercise and mark. Unit 27 examines all four competences.

body: Purpose: to introduce communicative competence as one goal with four parts. Content: a circle in four quarters labelled ‘Grammatical: the forms’, ‘Sociolinguistic: right for the situation’, ‘Discourse: connected text’ and ‘Strategic: getting round the gaps’, with ‘Communication’ at the centre. Style: clean, four muted colours. Board version: a circle divided by two lines, with four labels.

pts: Organises learning around real-world tasks with a clear outcome, not language exercises for their own sake.
The task cycle — pre-task, task, planning, report, language focus — structures a full lesson around doing, not drilling.
This builds directly on Tier I's task-based grammar preview in Unit 6.
points.who: Jane Willis, "A Framework for Task-Based Learning"

v: A handout with three picnic spots, costs and travel times

items: Pre-task: show a photo of a school picnic and explain that each group must plan one within a budget.
Task: groups of four agree on a plan. Monitor without correcting.
Planning: each group prepares a one-minute report with reasons.
Report: three or four groups report; the class votes for the best plan.
Language focus: write four useful sentences you heard on the board and work on one form learners needed.
Plan a class assembly or a stall for the school fair instead.
Support: a plan grid (place, cost, transport, food).
Challenge: add a constraint mid-task (Rain is forecast. Change your plan.).

lines: Cubbon Park: bus ₹20, free entry, 30 minutes. Nandi Hills: bus ₹60, entry ₹10, 90 minutes. Budget: ₹100 per learner.
A: Nandi Hills is nice but it is far.
B: And costly. Sixty plus ten is seventy. Food also we need.

blocks.x: Meaning comes first and language focus last. Unit 28 explains the full cycle (Willis 1996).

Purpose: to show the stages of a task-based lesson. Content: five linked boxes, ‘Pre-task’, ‘Task’, ‘Planning’, ‘Report’, ‘Language focus’, each with a small icon (a lightbulb, a group, a notebook, a speaker, a magnifying glass). Style: clear, flowing. Board version: five boxes joined by arrows.

pts: Fluency, accuracy and complexity compete for a learner's limited attention in real time — gains in one can cost another.
Different task designs deliberately push toward different points in this trilogy.
Planning time before a task measurably shifts output toward more fluency and complexity.

items: Half the pairs begin a two-minute talk on a picture immediately.
The other half get three minutes of silent planning (notes only) first.
A few pairs from each half perform.
Ask the class: who spoke more smoothly, used more ideas, made fewer mistakes?
Next lesson, swap the halves with a new picture.
Record two pairs on a phone and compare.
Support: a planning template (who, what happened, what next).
Challenge: include one sentence with because and one with although.

lines: S1: With planning I knew what to say next.
S2: Without planning I was fast but I made more mistakes.

blocks.x: Planning time tends to increase fluency and complexity, with more mixed effects on accuracy. Unit 29 reviews this research and Peter Skehan’s account of why attention must be shared between the three dimensions.

body: Purpose: to show competition for limited attention. Content: a learner at the centre of a triangle, pulled by three ropes towards ‘Fluency’, ‘Accuracy’ and ‘Complexity’; a bucket labelled ‘Attention’ is only partly full. Style: light, slightly humorous. Board version: a triangle with three labels.

items: Classroomscreen (free basic plan) for a visible timer.

blocks.x: The teacher’s watch; the teacher announces time.

pts: Real communication breakdowns and repairs — negotiation of meaning — are argued to be where acquisition actively happens.
Tasks with a genuine information gap generate far more negotiation than tasks with none.
This extends Tier I's Interaction Hypothesis preview (Unit 3) into the tier's core methodology.

items: Learner A gets one picture, Learner B the other; they must not show each other.
Write three repair phrases on the board (see model language).
Pairs describe and ask questions to find the differences.
Check as a class, then ask which repair phrases pairs actually used.
Draw two versions of a market scene on the two halves of the board; half the class faces away from each.
Support: a word bank of objects and positions.
Challenge: no pointing, and an eight-minute limit.

lines: Sorry, can you say that again? / What do you mean by…? / So there are three…, right?
A: In my picture the man has a big umbrella.
B: Umbrella? What colour?
A: Red. He is near the tea shop.
B: Oh, near the tea shop. In mine, no umbrella.

blocks.x: Neither learner can finish without the other. Unit 30 explores negotiation of meaning (Long 1996).

body: Purpose: to show an information-gap task. Content: two learners back to back, each holding a picture of a busy bus stand that differs in small details; speech bubbles carry a question and a clarification request. Style: lively. Board version: two simple drawings with small changes.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for making A and B pictures.

blocks.x: Hand-drawn pictures, photocopied or drawn on the board.

pts: Extensive reading and listening move from occasional supplementary practice into a core, scheduled part of the course.
Comprehensible input, provided in volume, is argued to be a necessary condition for acquisition.
This scales up Tier I's introduction of extensive reading (Unit 3) into a full methodology.

items: Collect forty to sixty easy books: graded readers, magazines, donated and learner-made books.
Fix a ten-minute slot at least three times a week.
Learners choose freely and read silently; the teacher reads too.
Learners write the title and a one-line response in a reading log.
Once a fortnight, learners recommend a book to a partner.
Replace reading with a short audio story played from the teacher’s phone.
Support: picture books and bilingual texts.
Challenge: longer books and a monthly target.

lines: 12 July. ‘The Moon and the Cap’. Funny. The monkey copied the man. 3 out of 5.

blocks.x: The rule of thumb is ‘easy, enjoyable and a lot’ (Day and Bamford 1998). Unit 31 builds a full programme; Unit 32 does the same for listening.

body: Purpose: to show input in volume. Content: a river of small open books flowing towards a learner reading under a tree, with a signpost ‘Easy, enjoyable, a lot’. Style: calm, rural Indian setting. Board version: not applicable.

items: StoryWeaver (free, Pratham Books) for openly licensed stories in English and many Indian languages.

blocks.x: A cardboard box library of donated and learner-made books.

pts: Real texts belong to genres — emails, reports, stories — each with predictable structure beyond individual sentences.
Discourse-level awareness helps learners produce and comprehend coherent, connected language, not just correct sentences.
This previews the deeper genre-based writing work coming in Tier III.

v: Six short texts of different genres

items: Give each group six short texts: a notice, an invitation, a recipe, a story opening, a news report and a friendly email.
Groups name each genre and underline the clues that helped them.
Build a class table of genre features.
Groups write a new text in one genre on a class topic.
Use real local texts: a wedding invitation, a bus ticket, a school circular.
Support: three genres instead of six.
Challenge: rewrite the news report as a friendly email.

lines: Recipe: a list, then imperatives (Add…, Stir…).
Invitation: You are cordially invited…, a date, a time, a place.
News report: a headline, past tense, who–what–where–when in the first sentence.

blocks.x: Knowing a genre helps learners predict when reading and plan when writing. Unit 33 develops genre awareness; Unit 54 teaches the genre-based writing cycle.

body: Purpose: to show genres as recognizable shapes. Content: six text silhouettes (a recipe with a list, a centred invitation, a news report with a headline and columns, an email with a subject line), words blurred so only the shape shows. Style: minimal grey outlines. Board version: quick rectangle sketches.

items: Google Docs (free) for preparing the texts.

blocks.x: Real printed materials collected by learners.

pts: Structured cooperative learning treats group work as a deliberate methodology, not just a classroom management technique.
Positive interdependence and individual accountability distinguish genuine cooperative learning from simple group seating.
This builds on Tier I's grouping dynamics (Unit 7, Unit 15) into a fuller methodological approach.
points.who: David & Roger Johnson's cooperative learning research

items: Form home groups of four; give each member one part of a text about four Indian scientists.
Learners with the same part meet as experts and agree on three key points.
Experts return home and teach their part.
Each home group completes a comparison table that needs all four parts.
Give a short individual quiz on all four parts.
Use four regions of India or four steps of a science process.
Support: easier parts for some experts, with a glossary.
Challenge: prepare two ‘why’ questions for each expert.

lines: S1: My scientist is Asima Chatterjee. She worked on medicines from plants.
S2: Which year was she born?

blocks.x: The group needs every part (positive interdependence), and the quiz checks each learner (individual accountability). These features distinguish cooperative learning from group seating (Johnson and Johnson 1989). Unit 34 develops the approach.

body: Purpose: to show the jigsaw structure. Content: four home groups of four coloured figures; arrows show same-coloured members moving to expert groups and back. Style: diagrammatic, bright. Board version: circles with numbers and arrows.

items: Padlet (free plan) for expert groups to post key points.

blocks.x: Text parts on paper; expert groups meet along bench rows.

body: With fixed benches, form home groups by turning two learners round to face the two behind them. Form expert groups by row, so learners move only along their bench.

pts: Teaching content — science, history, current events — through English integrates language learning with real subject matter.
Even a light version, used occasionally, increases the authenticity and cognitive demand of language use.
Full CLIL methodology is covered in depth later in this tier.

items: Show the diagram; learners name what they know in any language.
Teach four terms with gestures: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection.
Pairs label the diagram and order four sentences.
Pairs explain the cycle to another pair with first, then, after that, finally.
Ask one content question and one language question.
Plan the lesson with the science teacher, using the same diagram.
Support: key terms with Kannada or Hindi equivalents on the board.
Challenge: add a sentence about what happens in a drought.

blocks.x: A model paragraph (written for this book):

lines: First, the sun heats water in rivers and seas, and it evaporates. Then the vapour rises, cools and condenses into clouds. After that, water falls as rain. Finally, it collects in rivers and the sea, and the cycle begins again.

blocks.x: Even a light, occasional content lesson raises the authenticity and cognitive demand of English use. Unit 37 introduces CLIL (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010), and Unit 55 plans a full content unit.

body: Purpose: to show subject and language integrated. Content: a water-cycle diagram with four labelled stages; beside it, a column of sequence words and key terms with small home-language equivalents. Style: textbook-clear, blue and green. Board version: sun, cloud, rain and river with labels.

body: Look at one lesson you taught this week through the eight strands of this unit. Which does it already use? Add one missing strand, such as an information gap or a report stage, the next time you teach it.

dek: Unit 26 of 100: Tier II opens. Where Tier I built one strong lesson and one strong unit, Tier II integrates the four skills fully through task, interaction and extensive input.

aims.x: This unit opens Part II. Part I treated sounds, vocabulary, grammar and the four skills as separate, teachable pieces. Part II puts the pieces back together, because real communication uses them all at once. The unit is a map: each point introduces one strand of integrated teaching and names the later unit that treats it in full.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain communicative competence as the broad goal of Part II;
outline the task cycle;
describe how fluency, accuracy and complexity compete for attention;
explain why negotiation of meaning is thought to support acquisition;
plan a small, regular extensive reading slot;
recognize genre as a level of language above the sentence;
distinguish cooperative learning from simply seating learners in groups;
try a short lesson that teaches subject content through English.

why: Why this matters. Foundations taught skills and systems as separate, teachable pieces. Real communication uses them all at once — Tier II is where they recombine.

background.x: In 1972 the sociolinguist Dell Hymes argued that knowing a language means more than knowing its grammar: a speaker must also know what to say, to whom, when and in what manner (Hymes 1972). Michael Canale and Merrill Swain (1980) turned this idea into a model for language teaching and testing, later refined into four components: grammatical, sociolinguistic, discourse and strategic competence. If communication is the goal, a course that teaches only grammar is teaching one part of it.

Several methodological answers followed. Task-based teaching organizes lessons around meaningful work with an outcome (Prabhu 1987; Willis 1996). Research on interaction suggests that the breakdowns and repairs of real conversation help learners notice what they do not yet know (Long 1996). Research on input, associated especially with Stephen Krashen, argues that learners need very large amounts of language they can understand. Cooperative learning research shows how group work can be designed so that every learner contributes (Johnson and Johnson 1989). These strands differ in theory but share one message: learners acquire a language by using it for purposes that matter to them.

India has an important place in this story. N. S. Prabhu’s Communicational Teaching Project, run with teachers in South Indian schools from 1979 to 1984, was one of the first large trials of task-based teaching (Prabhu 1987). Today the NEP 2020 and the NCF 2023 call for experiential, competency-based learning and for home languages to be used as a resource (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020; NCERT 2023). Integrated teaching fits these aims well, provided it is adapted to classes of forty to sixty learners on fixed benches, with few devices and an exam at the end of the year.

items: Task outcome. Assess whether groups reached a workable outcome, not only whether their language was accurate.
Integrated performance. Use one task combining reading, speaking and writing, such as the water cycle, and note performance in each skill.
Reading logs. Check the number of books read and the quality of responses each month.
Teacher audit. Repeat the competence audit at the end of term.
Which of the four competences does your teaching develop most? Which least?
When did your learners last do a task with a real outcome?
Do your speaking activities contain a genuine gap?
How much English do your learners read or hear outside the textbook each week?
Is your group work cooperative in the technical sense?
Which subject colleague could you plan one joint lesson with?

terms.def: The knowledge and ability needed to use language appropriately in real situations, including grammar, social appropriacy, discourse and strategy, not only grammatical correctness (Hymes 1972).
An approach in which a subject such as science or geography is taught through an additional language, with planned attention to both content and language.
Structured group work in which learners depend on one another to achieve a shared goal, while each remains individually accountable.

Reading large quantities of easy, self-selected material for pleasure and general understanding, such as graded readers or StoryWeaver books (Day and Bamford 1998). It builds fluency, vocabulary and reading habits.
A type of text with a recognized social purpose and typical stages and language, such as a recount, a complaint letter, a lab report or a nursing handover.
In cooperative learning, the principle that each member is responsible for their own learning and contribution, checked for example by an individual quiz after group work.
The interactional work, such as clarification requests and comprehension checks, that speakers do to resolve breakdowns in understanding; it is claimed to help acquisition (Long 1996).
In cooperative learning, a condition in which group members need one another to succeed, so that each member’s contribution matters (Johnson and Johnson 1989).

Combining two or more language skills in one activity or sequence, as in real life, for example reading a notice, discussing it and writing a reply. Integration makes practice more meaningful and helps skills support each other.
The central phase of a task-based lesson, in which learners do the task, plan a report and present it to the class (Willis 1996). It is preceded by a pre-task and followed by a language focus.
